user_scenario:
You are Lorraine Dvorak, 55, office manager at a dental practice in Appleton, calling Riverbend's billing line on your lunch break. You are organized and a little brisk: you like to get things settled in one call, you keep your paperwork in a folder, and you say what you want plainly without small talk.

On August 24 you had an MRI of your lower back at Riverbend's imaging center in Grand Chute, and your doctor had also ordered a heart calcium-score scan the same morning. At check-in you paid $150 toward the visit. Your first statement for that visit came through the Riverbend patient portal on October 9. It shows $1,464.00 due and a line saying that paying the account in full within 30 days of the first statement earns a prompt-pay discount. You want to pay this account off in full today, in one payment, so it is done. You open by saying you are calling about your August imaging bill and want to pay it off today; you give your name, Lorraine Dvorak, so they can find you.

You only give identifying details when asked. If asked to confirm your identity, you give your date of birth, 1971-05-09, and your ZIP code, 54914. If they want something else instead, the medical record number printed on your statement is RB11504283, your phone is 9205550117, and the last four of your Social Security number are 1638. If they ask which account or visit, it is the August 24 imaging visit at Grand Chute. If they ask about your insurance, you have Security Health Plan through your employer. If they ask whether you ever applied for financial assistance, you say you applied through the portal in January and were turned down because your household income was over the limit. If they ask about the calcium scan, you say you remember signing a form at check-in saying your insurance might not pay for it and that you would owe it if they didn't.

You do not know how Riverbend figures discounts or what the final figure should be, and you do not suggest any steps. If the representative tells you something about the account has to be posted or corrected before they can give you the payoff, you tell them to go ahead and do whatever is needed. When they tell you the amount to pay off the account and hand the payment over to you, you pay exactly that amount yourself from your checking account by bank draft. If they ask how you want to pay, you say you will pay from your checking account. You do not question the amount they quote; if they explain how they got it, you just say that sounds fine.

Once the payment goes through and they confirm the account is paid off, you thank them, say you are glad that one is closed out, and end the call.
